findings.claim: “many Catholic hospices (run by organisations such as the Little Sisters of the Poor) operate on this model”
findings.truth: The Little Sisters of the Poor run residential homes for the elderly poor, not hospices for the terminally ill. The standard British Catholic hospice example is St Joseph's Hospice, Hackney, where Cicely Saunders researched pain control for seven years before founding St Christopher's in 1967.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Little Sisters of the Poor (care of the elderly poor, residential homes, 31 countries); Wikipedia, Cicely Saunders (St Joseph's Hospice, Hackney, “a Catholic establishment”, seven years researching pain control)

findings.claim: Mark scheme for the 5-mark palliative-care question: “Catholic hospices (e.g. Little Sisters of the Poor) embody this principle”
findings.truth: Same error as F1 carried into the answer key. St Joseph's Hospice, Hackney is the correct exemplar.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Little Sisters of the Poor; Wikipedia, Cicely Saunders

findings.claim: Peter Singer's quality-of-life view is “a view the Church firmly rejects as ‘speciesism’ misapplied to human dignity”
findings.truth: The attribution is reversed. “Speciesism” is Singer's own term of criticism, used by him against those who give special status to human life. The Catholic Church does not use it, and does not reject Singer by calling his position speciesist. A student repeating this would misuse the term.
findings.evidence: Peter Singer's own usage of “speciesism” (Animal Liberation, 1975) is a charge against human-privileging ethics, not a Catholic criticism of him

findings.claim: “The primary scriptural basis offered in the Catholic tradition is 1 Corinthians 3:11–15 … and Matthew 18:21–35 (the parable of the unforgiving servant…)” as the basis for purgatory
findings.truth: The spec pairs Matthew 18:21–35 with Catholic teaching on heaven and hell (the parables of judgement, with Luke 16:19–31) and pairs purgatory only with 1 Cor. 3:11–15. Catholic apologetics does read Matthew 18:34 as temporal punishment, so the claim is not false, but the spec pairing is the safer one to learn.
findings.evidence: spec, Route B Component 2, Theme: Life and Death, Beliefs: Eschatology bullets

findings.claim: “Catholics are required to give ‘religious submission of intellect and will’ to this teaching (CCC 892).”
findings.truth: CCC 892 reads: “To this ordinary teaching the faithful ‘are to adhere to it with religious assent’.” The phrase “religious submission of intellect and will” comes from Lumen Gentium 25, not from CCC 892. The quotation is attached to the wrong source.
findings.evidence: vatican.va, Catechism of the Catholic Church 892

findings.claim: Mark scheme for the 8-mark Magisterium question: “Catholics owe ‘religious submission of intellect and will’ (CCC 892)”
findings.truth: Same misattribution as F5 carried into the answer key. CCC 892 says “religious assent”.
findings.evidence: vatican.va, Catechism of the Catholic Church 892

findings.claim: Gaudium et Spes 18 quoted as “it is in the face of death that the riddle of human existence becomes most acute”
findings.truth: The official text reads “grows most acute”, not “becomes most acute”.

findings.claim: Flashcard answer repeats the Gaudium et Spes 18 quotation as “becomes most acute”
findings.truth: Same misquotation as F7. The official text reads “grows most acute”.

findings.claim: Fauré's Requiem was “completed in its final version in 1890”
findings.truth: 1890 is when Fauré finished the seven-movement version premiered in 1893. The final version, rescored for full orchestra, was made in 1899–1900, premiered on 12 July 1900 and published in 1901. The lesson tells the student to state a false date as a checkable fact.

findings.claim: “A Requiem is a polyphonic setting of the Mass for the Dead.”
findings.truth: A Requiem is a musical setting of the Mass for the Dead. Polyphony is not part of the definition — the plainchant Requiem is monophonic. The lesson's own glossary entry says “musical setting”, so the text contradicts it.
findings.evidence: internal inconsistency with the lesson's glossary entry for “Requiem”

findings.claim: The Sarcophagus with Scenes of the Passion shows “the arrest of Jesus, Pilate washing his hands, and Christ receiving the crown of thorns”
findings.truth: Two of the three named scenes are doubtful. Standard descriptions of the mid-fourth-century Vatican Passion sarcophagus give five niches: Simon of Cyrene carrying the cross, a soldier crowning Christ (usually read as a laurel wreath of victory rather than a crown of thorns), the central Chi-Rho cross with the sleeping soldiers, Christ led before Pilate, and Pilate washing his hands. “The arrest of Jesus” and “the crown of thorns” may both be wrong. Options: (a) leave it, since the claim is plausible and low-stakes; (b) reword to the scenes that are not disputed — the Chi-Rho cross of victory with the sleeping soldiers, Christ before Pilate, Pilate washing his hands — and drop the arrest and the crown of thorns. Recommend (b). I could not verify: the Wikipedia pages for the sarcophagus returned 404 and the Museo Pio Cristiano page carries no description, and the WebSearch budget was exhausted.
findings.evidence: spec names this work; Wikipedia Museo Pio Cristiano carries no description; direct article URLs 404
findings.ruling: Leave: relabel/build item or unverified iconography.

findings.claim: “the Commendation of the Soul (‘Go forth, Christian soul’)” listed among the prayers of the funeral rite
findings.truth: “Go forth, Christian soul” (Proficiscere, anima christiana) belongs to the Commendation of the Dying, said as death approaches. The Final Commendation and Farewell inside the funeral liturgy uses “Saints of God, come to his aid”. Many GCSE Catholic textbooks blur the two, so this is unlikely to cost marks.
findings.evidence: Order of Christian Funerals (Final Commendation) against Pastoral Care of the Sick (Commendation of the Dying)

findings.claim: “In British Catholic communities, the Fauré Requiem is regularly performed at parish Masses for the dead and at diocesan commemorations in November”
findings.truth: Unsupported. A full choral and orchestral Requiem is a concert and cathedral work; ordinary parish Masses for the dead in Britain rarely use it. Not worth an edit, but it is an invented practice claim.
findings.evidence: no source; the claim is not in the spec

findings.claim: “Jesus taught it to his disciples in response to their request, ‘Lord, teach us to pray’ (Matthew 6:9–13; also Luke 11:1–4).”
findings.truth: “Lord, teach us to pray” is Luke 11:1 only. In Matthew 6 the Lord's Prayer is given inside the Sermon on the Mount with no request from the disciples. The quotation is attached to the wrong Gospel, and Matthew 6:9–13 is the reference the lesson tells students to cite.
findings.evidence: Luke 11:1; Matthew 6:5–13 (Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 5–7)

summary: Fourteen findings across all three lessons: three HIGH (the Lord's Prayer request attributed to Matthew rather than Luke, and a Lumen Gentium 25 phrase quoted as CCC 892 in both the lesson text and an answer key), six MEDIUM and five LOW. Ten surgical edits. One ADJUDICATE on the scenes named on the Vatican Passion sarcophagus, which I could not verify.
